transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-12 15:00 PST
Duration: ~1h15m
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (SE), Ethan (Solutions Eng), Carlos (Nexera CTO), Priya (ML), Liam (Infra), Aisha (Data)

Auto-summary (auto): quick deep dive on rerank pipeline economics and ops.

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, with Maya and Ethan. Quick roll call?
00:08 Carlos: Carlos here, CTO at Nexera.
:12 Priya: Priya - ML eng.
:15 Liam: Liam infra.
:17 Aisha: Aisha data science.
00:20 Jordan: Great. Goal for today is to map out cost/latency tradeoffs for candidate reranking — you've said you're evaluating embedding dims, batch sizes, and thinking about running this on-prem. Correct?
00:30 Carlos: Yep. We run an ANN approximator for candidate generation, then a reranker that scores top-N with a small cross-encoder on GPU. We want sub-100ms average and p99 under 500ms for user-facing flows, and cost under X (they didn't want to commit yet).
00:45 Maya: Quick clarifying question — are you performing rerank with bi-encoder dot products only, or doing full cross-encoder re-score on the top-K?
00:52 Priya: Top-K cross-encoder for final ranking, K is usually 50 right now. We push candidate generation to offline when possible but user-facing queries need on-demand rerank.
01:05 Ethan: Ok that changes batching assumptions — cross-encoder is sequence-pair input so KV cache is not used the same way as autoregressive generation. KV cache talk is more relevant if you were doing LLM prefix caching for prompt-based rerank. For embeddings/pure bi-encoder dot-product rerank, it's dense matrix multiply mostly.
01:22 Liam: A few infra constraints: on-prem cluster is 4xA10 GPUs per rack, 96GB RAM per host, 10Gbps interconnect, and strict firewall. We want to avoid egress where possible.
01:36 Jordan: Good context. Let's break this into three buckets: 1) candidate generation & ANN cost (we'll assume you have that covered), 2) embedding dimension choice (memory, throughput, nearest-neighbor index size), 3) reranker compute (batching, quantization, tail latency).

03:10 Maya: Starting with embedding dims: smaller dims (like 128/256) reduce ANN storage and ANN query time and are cheaper to compute per embed, but you lose retrieval quality for nuanced semantic similarity. 768-dim and 1536-dim are common tradeoffs; 1536 gives more headroom but costs ~2x memory and compute compared to 768. In our internal benchmarks a 1536-dim index was ~1.9x larger and single-query ANN seek latency grew by ~1.3x depending on index type.
03:48 Priya: We're worried about index size — we have 500M docs. Can you ballpark storage?
03:53 Maya: Roughly: 500M x 768 x 4 bytes (float32) ~ 1.5TB raw vectors; with product quantization or float16 you can cut that by 4x or more. For 1536 it's proportionally higher. Also indexes like HNSW have additional overhead. If you use IVF+PQ you get big compaction but with more recall tuning.
04:28 Aisha: If we compress embeddings aggressively with PQ/8-bit we see some drop in rerank accuracy — how severe is that for your use case?
04:33 Maya: Empirically for reranking, PQ 8-bit on 768 dims can be ~1.5-3% drop in top1/top5 depending on dataset. For cross-encoder final scoring it's less impactful because the cross-encoder provides final judgment, but it affects candidate recall which constrains cross-encoder effectiveness.

05:20 Ethan: On the reranker compute: cross-encoders are expensive. If you're running K=50, each query becomes 50 forward passes (or batch those). Batching is the primary lever: GPUs are throughput-optimized, so larger batch sizes increase GPU utilization and lower per-query cost, but increase latency for individual queries.
05:45 Liam: We need hard numbers: what's p95/p99 for 4xA10 with batch sizes of 8/16/32 for a 340M-parameter cross-encoder?
05:56 Maya: Rough numbers from internal runs: batch=8 -> avg latency ~90ms per batch item; p95 ~220ms; p99 ~420ms. batch=16 -> avg ~65ms; p95 ~180ms; p99 ~380ms. batch=32 -> avg ~45ms; p95 ~160ms; p99 ~350ms. But these numbers depend strongly on sequence length and model architecture, and batching introduces queueing delay if you wait to fill the batch.
06:30 Carlos: Those p99s are close to our 500ms ceiling. But the queuing wait time will push p99 up. How does Redwood handle async batching and tail isolation?
06:40 Maya: Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLO safeties — you can set max batch wait (e.g., 5-20ms) and a priority lane for low-latency queries that bypass batching. There's also burst isolation across tenants on Dedicated. For on-prem we can replicate the same runtime and policy but you'll manage autoscaling.
07:05 Priya: What about KV cache? We historically used KV cache for streaming LLMs, but for rerank cross-encoders it's not applicable, right?
07:12 Ethan: Correct—KV cache is for autoregressive token caching. For pairwise cross-encoding there's essentially no KV reuse between different queries; caching helps more for prefix-heavy generation or when you repeatedly score same long contexts. For embeddings/batch dot-product workloads, caching vector shards or prefetching indices is more relevant.
07:32 Aisha: We do have a hybrid: sometimes we do a light LLM-based prompt to generate query expansion, then embed that. Could KV cache help there?
07:40 Maya: Slightly — if you do autoregressive prompt generation repeatedly for the same user session, KV caching reduces token compute; but remember that adds infra complexity and may shift cost from vector compute to autoregressive. Often simpler to do deterministic expansion offline or maintain a short-circuit of top lexical matches.

09:00 Jordan: Let's talk quantization for reranker models and embeddings. Two axes: quantize the embeddings (storage & ANN) and quantize the reranker model weights (FP16->INT8/4).
09:12 Maya: For embeddings: PQ/8-bit gives large index savings. For reranker weights: int8 quantization of the cross-encoder can reduce memory and increase throughput ~1.6-2x with modest quality loss if done with per-channel calibration. Some models tolerate 4-bit quant without large accuracy loss but it's model-dependent and you need evals.
09:35 Priya: Do you have automated eval harnesses to test QA/mean reciprocal rank drop when applying quantization?
09:41 Ethan: Yes, Redwood Optimize includes a quality monitoring harness you can run: it will run your eval set across baseline float32 and quantized variants and report delta metrics. We recommended running it on your rerank dev set (we can help).

11:02 Liam: Networking question: if we run on-prem and still want occasional fallbacks to hosted (for overflow), how does traffic egress work? Our policy blocks outgoing traffic to third-party endpoints except through a controlled NAT. Egress costs are also a concern.
11:20 Jordan: Typical pattern: local on-prem handles normal load; Redwood Dedicated/Hosted is used as a fallback via an encrypted tunnel or VPN. We'll provide an egress estimate; with 10k QPS overflow at 1k tokens average, egress could cost materially, so we usually recommend reserved burst budgets or a regional dedicated failover to minimize cross-cloud egress.

13:00 Maya: Let's run through a cost example at a high level — assume 500k user-facing rerank queries/month, K=50, cross-encoder float32 baseline. Each query = 50 forward passes. If your cross-encoder amortized GPU throughput is 300 inferences/sec (per GPU) at batch-optimal settings, you can approximate GPU hours and then translate to cost. We prepared a simple sheet in the benchmark link we shared.
13:33 Carlos: We need a per-1M-queries cost comparison hosted vs dedicated vs on-prem including infra ops headcount. Can you add that to the sheet?
13:39 Jordan: Yes — action item. We'll add a row for ops FTE assumptions and amortized hardware replacement.

15:10 Priya: On tail-latency mitigation: suggestions?
15:13 Maya: Several levers: 1) hybrid batching (small max wait + priority lane), 2) pre-warming a small pool of warmed GPU workers for interactive traffic to reduce cold-start tail, 3) small-batch local CPU for very short queries, 4) guarding K (choose K such that cross-encoder cost is tractable for p99), 5) use distilled/smaller cross-encoder for top-of-funnel filtering.
15:40 Aisha: We tried reducing K to 20, we lost some downstream metric — click-through on recommendations down ~6%. So recall matters a lot. Can we do a two-stage rerank: cheap bi-encoder filter then cross-encoder on top 20?
15:52 Ethan: That's recommended — a cheap bi-encoder or lexical scorer can triage to a smaller candidate K for the cross-encoder. That reduces 90% of cross-encoder compute and preserves most quality if recall of the cheap filter is high. Also consider asymmetric indexing: heavy index for offline, and light in online.

18:00 Liam: For on-prem install windows — what infra specs do you recommend? 4xA10 per availability zone? SSD local NVMe for ANN shards?
18:10 Maya: Yes NVMe for index shards, GPUs depending on throughput: A10s are solid for mixed workloads; if you want denser throughput consider A100s or H100s (costly). For inter-node bandwidth, 25Gbps is preferable for cross-node gather if you distribute K shards. Keep at least 256GB disk per host for index replicas.
18:33 Jordan: Also note the runtime supports shard-local ANN lookups to limit cross-node traffic. For replicas and high availability plan 2-3 replicas per shard.

20:05 Carlos: Security/compliance: SOC2, SSO, audit logs — we need full pack.
20:12 Jordan: We'll drop the SOC2 and SSO docs in the shared link. For on-prem, audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.

22:00 Priya: Quick question on model versioning: if we roll quantized reranker in prod and see drift, can Redwood automatically rollback?
22:10 Ethan: Yes — Redwood Console supports model pinning and rollout policies: canary %, automatic rollback on quality regression connected to your eval set or prompt-set. We'll help set that up.

24:00 Maya: Ok, to make this actionable: we'll run two bench sets — one measuring throughput/cost for three embedding dims (256/768/1536) focusing on ANN index size and recall; second measuring cross-encoder latency curves across batch sizes and quant levels (fp16, int8). We'll simulate real arrival patterns (bursty) to see p99 effects.
24:25 Carlos: Good. Also include a scenario with K=20 and two-stage pipeline to compare end-to-end user metric proxies.
24:32 Jordan: Done.
